title: The Legacy of Muslim Rule in India
lede: Lal, a senior historian of the Delhi Sultanate, writes a social history of medieval India from the Persian chronicles and European travellers. He describes a theocratic state run by a foreign-descended nobility in great luxury, a middle class of merchants who dared not look rich, and a peasantry squeezed until it ran away. His conclusion is that the lasting legacy of five centuries of Muslim rule is not a composite culture but “medievalism”, and a division between Hindus and Muslims that living together never healed.

note: Lal's account stresses exploitation and religious division. Other historians, for example of the Aligarh school, describe the same society as more mixed, with shared institutions and culture. This page summarises his interpretation, attributed to him.

A closed aristocracy, mostly of foreign descent, living in luxury “not dreamt of even by kings in Persia” (Jadunath Sarkar).
Wealth hidden for safety, lest they be “used as filled sponges” (Edward Terry). Protest through the bhakti movements.
“Unmitigated exploitation”. Flight was the peasant's “first answer to famine or man's oppression”, as Babur saw whole villages vanish and reappear.

sections.title: What Lal thinks remains
items: Mixing in food, dress, architecture and music, but “a superficial veneer”.
“Even living together for a thousand years has not welded Hindus and Muslims into one people.”
Dar al-Islam and dar al-harb live on, he argues, citing Deoband fatwas.
Pakistan “solved its minority problem”, he says, and India did not.
